    return NormalizedMessage(
        role=role,

A realistic defect (SM-9B37A894) changes it to:
def normalize_content(content: object, *, role: ChatRole = "user") -> NormalizedMessage:
    """Normalize role-less public content into one provider-neutral message."""
    return NormalizedMessage(
        role="user",
        parts=normalize_parts(_content_parts(content)),
        meta={},
    )
What the defect does: Role argument is ignored: normalized message is always created with the default "user" role, so caller-supplied roles (assistant/system) are lost.. What the test must check: Call normalize_content with a role other than "user" (for example role="model") and check that the returned NormalizedMessage's role equals that argument.
On this input the two differ: normalize_content(content="hello", role="model")
The original gives ('dataclass', 'NormalizedMessage', {'role': 'model', 'parts': [('dataclass', 'TextPart', {'kind': 'text', 'text': 'hello'})], 'meta': {}}); the defect gives ('dataclass', 'NormalizedMessage', {'role': 'user', 'parts': [('dataclass', 'TextPart', {'kind': 'text', 'text': 'hello'})], 'meta': {}}).
What it calls in its module:
def normalize_parts(parts: Sequence[ChatPart]) -> tuple[NormalizedPart, ...]:
    """Normalize public message parts while preserving caller order."""
    normalized: list[NormalizedPart] = []
    for part in parts:
        if isinstance(part, str):
            normalized.append(TextPart(kind="text", text=part))
        else:
            normalized.append(MediaPart(kind="media", media=describe_media(part)))
    return tuple(normalized)
def _content_parts(content: object) -> tuple[ChatPart, ...]:
    """Return public content as ordered parts."""
    if isinstance(content, str):
        return (content,)
    if isinstance(content, Sequence) and not isinstance(content, bytes | bytearray):
        return tuple(content)

    msg = f"Unsupported message content: {type(content).__name__}."
    raise TypeError(msg)
